title: Work practice
hook: cleaning, gardening and cooking as meditation

segments.voice: Yesterday: oryoki, the nested bowls, and your line, just enough. Did you notice how much was enough at one meal? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

The tools have gone missing. That's how a story about the Chan teacher Baizhang begins, as tradition tells it. He's old, and his students worry about him working in the fields, so they hide his hoe and his rake. Baizhang doesn't argue. He just doesn't eat that day. When they ask why, the answer that has come down is short: a day without work is a day without food. The tools come back. In Zen monasteries today, there's a whole period set aside for exactly what Baizhang refused to give up. Today's word: samu.
screen: `THE TOOLS GO MISSING.` → `THE OLD TEACHER WON'T EAT.` → `NO WORK, NO FOOD.`

segments.voice: First, what samu is. It's the work period in a Zen monastery or retreat: sweeping, raking, scrubbing floors, weeding, chopping vegetables, cleaning toilets. It's done in silence, usually for a set stretch of the day, and everyone takes part, teachers included. Second, why work counts as practice. The idea isn't that chores are a break from meditation. It's that meditation doesn't stop when you pick up a broom. The same attention that watched the breath now watches the bristles on the floor, the water in the bucket, the weed coming up with its roots. Samu takes the mind trained on the cushion and puts it to work in the world. Third, the attitude. In samu nobody is meant to rush to finish, and nobody picks the nice job. You're handed a task and you do it fully, whether it's polishing a statue or unclogging a drain. Some teachers say the toilets are a good place to see your own mind: what you resist is right there in the bucket. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. Baizhang's line ties the meal to the work, and the work to the way. Feeding the community, keeping it clean, is the practice, not a distraction from it. So a sink full of dishes isn't standing between you and practice. It might be the practice, if you let it.
screen: `SWEEPING, WEEDING, SCRUBBING.` · `THE BROOM IS THE CUSHION NOW.` · `NO NICE JOBS, NO RUSHING.` · `THE DISHES MIGHT BE THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `WORK IS ZEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Find one small thing within reach that could be cleaner: a phone screen, a cup, a corner of the table, your glasses. Clean it, slowly, with full attention. Feel the cloth or your sleeve against the surface. Notice the moment your mind wants to hurry, or drift to the next thing. Come back to this one surface. When it's clean, set it down, and sit with the breath for whatever time remains. The bell holds the time.
Samu. Work practice in Zen: cleaning, gardening, cooking, done in silence and with full attention, as meditation in motion. Today's word.
Your line: work is zen. Today, take one chore you usually rush, dishes, laundry, the trash, and do it as samu: silent, unhurried, all the way to the end. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: In Zen monasteries and at many retreats, a daily work period called samu has everyone, teachers included, clean, garden and cook in silence, treating the work as meditation rather than a break from it.
